paras: The whitecapping on the Nevins farm was an attack by white men described as "white caps" on Black people living on the farm of H. H. Nevins in Barnwell County, South Carolina, in the summer of 1895. At least one Black man was whipped, and Nevins told the governor that all his hands had been driven from his place. The case drew attention because it reached Governor Evans during a wider run of whitecapping complaints from the county.

By August 1895 Governor Evans was receiving complaints about what A. H. Patterson of Barnwell called "the white-capping matter" in Barnwell County, where several cases had been reported. A Columbia dispatch in the Savannah Morning News said that the "whitecaps in Barnwell county are still causing some concern."

No paper gives a date for the attack; an item credited to the Register and reprinted on August 26 placed the beating "several weeks ago." According to A. H. Patterson of Barnwell, a "colored boy" was said to have been caught under a building looking at young girls and was let off on the understanding that his parents would whip him. When the boy's brother objected and interfered, "certain white persons" went to the place, took the brother out and whipped him.

Nevins gave a different picture in a telegram to the governor reported on August 17. He said all his hands had been driven off, that "a reign of terror" prevailed about his place, that he did not know what the white caps had against them, and that he would be ruined unless they returned.

Governor Evans ordered Sheriff Lancaster to investigate. Patterson said Nevins, "so it is said," took out warrants against some of the white men who did the whipping, fearing that such treatment would drive labor from his farm. Later a Black man in Barnwell wrote the governor imploring him "for God's sake" to protect them against the white caps and describing how a man had been tied up and beaten. The sheriff replied that he was "ferreting out the facts" and that all was quiet; no report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found.

The case was covered only in the white press, chiefly in the Savannah Morning News, which carried the farmer's complaint under the heading "The White Caps Still at Work in Parts of South Carolina," Patterson's account in its South Carolina column, and the Register's item calling the Black man's letter "pathetic." These items reported each version without comment, though Patterson's account carried the accusation against the boy that the other reports did not mention. The Sumter Watchman and Southron took a firmer line, writing that white caps were "persecuting a farmer by the name of Nevins" and that a few of them should be sent to Columbia and "supplied with striped pants." No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

Patterson told the governor there was "no organize band of white-caps" in the county and that each reported case stood "on their own bottom," while Nevins, the Watchman and Southron and the Black letter writer all attributed the trouble to "white caps." The farmer's name also appears as Nevils in Patterson's account and as Nevins in the other two reports.

reader.title: Whitecapping on the Nevins farm, Barnwell County
bases: Reports call the attackers 'white caps' who whipped or beat a Black man and drove the hands off a Barnwell County farm (A3, A5, A6), and Patterson describes a whipping by 'certain white persons' while denying an organized band (A4).

The farmer's telegram (A3), Patterson's account (A4) and the Register's report of a Black man's letter (A6) independently describe white-cap trouble and a beating connected to the case the governor sent Sheriff Lancaster to investigate; Patterson disputes only that an organized band was responsible.

accounts.label: Farmer's telegram
accounts.gist: Nevins said all his hands had been driven off, a reign of terror prevailed about his place, he did not know what the white caps had against his hands, and he would be ruined unless they returned.

accounts.label: Patterson's account
accounts.gist: There was no organized band; a Black boy caught looking at girls was to be whipped by his parents, his brother interfered, and white men took the brother out and whipped him, after which Nevins reportedly swore out warrants fearing his labor would leave.

accounts.label: Black letter writer (via the Register)
accounts.gist: A Black man begged the governor for protection against the 'white caps' and related that a negro had been tied up and beaten several weeks earlier.

framing.detail: The Watchman and Southron said 'a few of the white caps' should be put in 'striped pants' at work that would keep them 'out of devilment'.

The Savannah Morning News ran the case in Columbia dispatches and its South Carolina column under 'The White Caps Still at Work in Parts of South Carolina', giving the farmer's, Patterson's and the letter writer's versions without comment, and calling the letter 'pathetic'.

versions.value: No organized band of white-caps in the county; each case 'stand[s] on their own bottom'; 'certain white persons' whipped the brother

conflicts.note: Patterson's denial is one local man's claim made to the governor; the other reports adopt the 'white caps' label without giving names or numbers.
